entries.e69bc4d0e0aa4d1667775b10147f3fa167f53ba4: <div sID="gen32091" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Col.3" sID="Col.3"/> <div eID="gen32091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32092" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32093" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle exhorts us to set our hearts upon heaven and take them off from this world, <reference osisRef="Col.3.1-Col.3.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. He exhorts to the mortification of sin, in the various instances of it, <reference osisRef="Col.3.5-Col.3.11">ver. 5-11</reference>. III. He earnestly presses to mutual love and compassion, <reference osisRef="Col.3.12-Col.3.17">ver. 12-17</reference>. And concludes with exhortations to relative duties, of wives and husbands, parents and children, masters and servants, <reference osisRef="Col.3.18-Col.3.25">ver. 18-25</reference>.
entries.01373a55dc67330670e2efae92ab01afd219b4f3: <div eID="gen32093" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32092" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Spiritual Life. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32094" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God. <hi type="super">2</hi> Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth. <hi type="super">3</hi> For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God. <hi type="super">4</hi> When Christ, <hi type="italic">who is</hi> our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory. <div eID="gen32094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32095" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having described our privileges by Christ in the former part of the epistle, and our discharge from the yoke of the ceremonial law, comes here to press upon us our duty as inferred thence. Though we are made free from the obligation of the ceremonial law, it does not therefore follow that we may live as we list. We must walk the more closely with God in all the instances of evangelical obedience. He begins with exhorting them to set their hearts on heaven, and take them off from this world: <hi type="italic">If you then have risen with Christ.</hi> It is our privilege that we have risen with Christ; that is, have benefit by the resurrection of Christ, and by virtue of our union and communion with him are justified and sanctified, and shall be glorified. Hence he infers that we must <hi type="italic">seek those things which are above.</hi> We must mind the concerns of another world more than the concerns of this. We must make heaven our scope and aim, seek the favour of God above, keep up our communion with the upper world by faith, and hope, and holy love, and make it our constant care and business to secure our title to and qualifications for the heavenly bliss. And the reason is because <hi type="italic">Christ sits at the right hand of God.</hi> He who is our best friend and our head is advanced to the highest dignity and honour in heaven, and has gone before to secure to us the heavenly happiness; and therefore we should seek and secure what he has purchased at so vast an expense, and is taking so much care about. We must live such a life as Christ lived here on earth and lives now in heaven, according to our capacities. <div eID="gen32095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32096" type="x-p"/> I. He explains this duty (<reference osisRef="Col.3.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Set your affections on things above, not on things on the earth.</hi> Observe, To seek heavenly things is to set our affections upon them, to love them and let our desires be towards them. Upon the wings of affection the heart soars upwards, and is carried forth towards spiritual and divine objects. We must acquaint ourselves with them, esteem them above all other things, and lay out ourselves in preparation for the enjoyment of them. David gave this proof of his <hi type="italic">loving the house of God,</hi> that he diligently sought after it, and prepared for it, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>. This is to be spiritually minded (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.6">Rom. viii. 6</reference>), and to <hi type="italic">seek and desire a better country, that is, a heavenly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.14">Heb. xi. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Things on earth</hi> are here set in opposition to <hi type="italic">things above.</hi> We must not dote upon them, nor expect too much from them, that we may set our affections on heaven; for heaven and earth are contrary one to the other, and a supreme regard to both is inconsistent; and the prevalence of our affection to one will proportionably weaken and abate our affection to the other. <div eID="gen32096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32097" type="x-p"/> II. He assigns three reasons for this, <reference osisRef="Col.3.3-Col.3.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen32097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32098" type="x-p"/> 1. That we are dead; that is, to present things, and as our portion. We are so in profession and obligation; for we are <hi type="italic">buried with Christ, and planted into the likeness of his death.</hi> Every Christian is <hi type="italic">crucified unto the world,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the world is crucified unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.14">Gal. vi. 14</reference>. And if we are dead to the earth, and have renounced it as our happiness, it is absurd for us to <hi type="italic">set our affections</hi> upon it, and <hi type="italic">seek</hi> it. We should be like a dead thing to it, unmoved and unaffected towards it. <div eID="gen32098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32099" type="x-p"/> 2. Our true life lies in the other world: <hi type="italic">You are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">v. 3</reference>. The new man has its livelihood thence. It is born and nourished from above; and the perfection of its life is reserved for that state. It is <hi type="italic">hid with Christ;</hi> not hid from us only, in point of secrecy, but hid for us, denoting security. The life of a Christian <hi type="italic">is hid with Christ. Because I live you shall live also,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.19">John xiv. 19</reference>. Christ is at present a hidden Christ, or one <hi type="italic">whom we have not seen;</hi> but this is our comfort, that our <hi type="italic">life is hid with him,</hi> and laid up safely with him. As we have reason to <hi type="italic">love him whom we have not seen</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.8">1 Pet. i. 8</reference>), so we may take the comfort of a happiness out of sight, and <hi type="italic">reserved in heaven for us.</hi> <div eID="gen32099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32100" type="x-p"/> 3. Because at the second coming of Christ we hope for the perfection of our happiness. If we live a life of Christian purity and devotion now, <hi type="italic">when Christ, who is our life, shall appear, we shall also appear with him in glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.4">v. 4</reference>. Observe, (1.) Christ is a believer's life. <hi type="italic">I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Gal. ii. 20</reference>. He is the principle and end of the Christian's life. He lives <hi type="italic">in</hi> us by his Spirit, and we live to him in all we do. <hi type="italic">To me to live is Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.21">Phil. i. 21</reference>. (2.) Christ will appear again. He is now <hi type="italic">hid;</hi> and the <hi type="italic">heavens must contain</hi> him; but he will appear in all the pomp of the upper world, with his <hi type="italic">holy angels,</hi> and in <hi type="italic">his own glory and his Father's glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.8.38">Mark viii. 38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.26">Luke ix. 26</reference>. (3.) We shall then appear with him in glory. It will be his glory to have his redeemed with him; he will come to be glorified in his saints (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.10">2 Thess. i. 10</reference>); and it will be their glory to come with him, and be with him for ever. At the second coming of Christ there will be a general meeting of all the saints; and those whose life is now <hi type="italic">hid with Christ</hi> shall then appear with Christ in that glory which he himself enjoys, <reference osisRef="John.17.24">John xvii. 24</reference>. Do we look for such a happiness, and should we not set our affections upon that world, and live above this? What is there here to make us fond of it? What is there not there to draw our hearts to it? Our head is there, our home is there, our treasure is there, and we hope to be there for ever.
entries.d5c9ce6d15e498aa35d01d217ad61e91b31bfc95: <div eID="gen32100" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Necessity of Mortifying Sin. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32101" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry: <hi type="super">6</hi> For which things' sake the wrath of God cometh on the children of disobedience: <hi type="super">7</hi> In the which ye also walked some time, when ye lived in them. <div eID="gen32101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32102" type="x-p"/> The apostle exhorts the Colossians to the mortification of sin, the great hindrance to seeking the things which are above. Since it is our duty to set our affections upon heavenly things, it is our duty to mortify our <hi type="italic">members which are upon the earth,</hi> and which naturally incline us to the things of the world: "Mortify them, that is, subdue the vicious habits of mind which prevailed in your Gentile state. Kill them, suppress them, as you do weeds or vermin which spread and destroy all about them, or as you kill an enemy who fights against you and wounds you."—<hi type="italic">Your members which are upon the earth;</hi> either the members of the body, which are the earthly part of us, and were <hi type="italic">curiously wrought in the lower parts of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Ps. cxxxix. 15</reference>), or the corrupt affections of the mind, which lead us to earthly things, the members of the body of death, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">Rom. vii. 24</reference>. He specifies, <div eID="gen32102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32103" type="x-p"/> I. The lusts of the flesh, for which they were before so very remarkable: <hi type="italic">Fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence</hi>—the various workings of the carnal appetites and fleshly impurities, which they indulged in their former course of life, and which were so contrary to the Christian state and the heavenly hope. <div eID="gen32103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32104" type="x-p"/> II. The love of the world: <hi type="italic">And covetousness, which is idolatry;</hi> that is, an inordinate love of present good and outward enjoyments, which proceeds from too high a value in the mind, puts upon too eager a pursuit, hinders the proper use and enjoyment of them, and creates anxious fear and immoderate sorrow for the loss of them. Observe, Covetousness is spiritual idolatry: it is the giving of that love and regard to worldly wealth which are due to God only, and carries a greater degree of malignity in it, and is more highly provoking to God, than is commonly thought. And it is very observable that among all the instances of sin which good men are recorded in the scripture to have fallen into (and there is scarcely any but some or other, in one or other part of their life, have fallen into) there is no instance in all the scripture of any good man charged with covetousness. He proceeds to show how necessary it is to mortify sins, <reference osisRef="Col.3.6-Col.3.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. 1. Because, if we do not kill them, they will kill us: <hi type="italic">For which things' sake the wrath of God cometh on the children of disobedience,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.6">v. 6</reference>. See what we are all by nature more or less: we are <hi type="italic">children of disobedience:</hi> not only disobedient children, but under the power of sin and naturally prone to disobey. The <hi type="italic">wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray as soon as they are born, speaking lies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.58.3">Ps. lviii. 3</reference>. And, being children of disobedience, we are <hi type="italic">children of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.3">Eph. ii. 3</reference>. The wrath of God comes upon all the children of disobedience. Those who do not obey the precepts of the law incur the penalties of it. The sins he mentions were their sins in their heathen and idolatrous state, and they were then especially the children of disobedience; and yet these sins brought judgments upon them, and exposed them to the wrath of God. 2. We should mortify these sins because they have lived in us: <hi type="italic">In which you also walked some time, when you lived in them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.7">v. 7</reference>. Observe, The consideration that we have formerly lived in sin is a good argument why we should now forsake it. We have walked in by-paths, therefore let us walk in them no more. <hi type="italic">If I have done iniquity, I will do no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.34.32">Job xxxiv. 32</reference>. The time past our lives may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1 Pet. iv. 3</reference>.—<hi type="italic">When you lived among those who did such things</hi> (so some understand it), then you walked in those evil practices. It is a hard thing to live among those who do the works of darkness and not have fellowship with them, as it is to walk in the mire and contract no soil. Let us keep out of the way of evil-doers.
entries.d22b2760e857755d57a3fdf0f78ee443d9c50ec0: <div eID="gen32104" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Necessity of Mortifying Sin. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32105" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth. 9 Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds; <hi type="super">10</hi> And have put on the new <hi type="italic">man,</hi> which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him: <hi type="super">11</hi> Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond <hi type="italic">nor</hi> free: but Christ <hi type="italic">is</hi> all, and in all. <div eID="gen32105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32106" type="x-p"/> As we are to mortify inordinate appetites, so we are to mortify inordinate passions (<reference osisRef="Col.3.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">But now you also put off all these, anger wrath, malice;</hi> for these are contrary to the design of the gospel, as well as grosser impurities; and, though they are more spiritual wickedness, have not less malignity in them. The gospel religion introduces a change of the higher as well as the lower powers of the soul, and supports the dominion of right reason and conscience over appetite and passion. Anger and wrath are bad, but malice is worse, because it is more rooted and deliberate; it is anger heightened and settled. And, as the corrupt principles in the heart must be cut off, so the product of them in the tongue; as <hi type="italic">blasphemy,</hi> which seems there to mean, not so much speaking ill of God as speaking ill of men, giving ill language to them, or raising ill reports of them, and injuring their good name by any evil arts,—<hi type="italic">filthy communication,</hi> that is, all lewd and wanton discourse, which comes from a polluted mind in the speaker and propagates the same defilements in the hearers,—and lying: <hi type="italic">Lie not one to another</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.3.9">v. 9</reference>), for it is contrary both to the law of truth and the law of love, it is both unjust and unkind, and naturally tends to destroy all faith and friendship among mankind. Lying makes us like the devil (who is the <hi type="italic">father of lies</hi>), and is a prime part of the devil's image upon our souls; and therefore we are cautioned against this sin by this general reason: Seeing <hi type="italic">you have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.10">v. 10</reference>. The consideration that we have by profession put away sin and espoused the cause and interest of Christ, that we have renounced all sin and stand engaged to Christ, should fortify us against this sin of lying. Those who have put off the old man have put it off with its deeds; and those who have put on the new man must put on all its deeds—not only espouse good principles but act them in a good conversation. The new man is said to be <hi type="italic">renewed in knowledge,</hi> because an ignorant soul cannot be a good soul. Without knowledge the heart cannot be good, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.2">Prov. xix. 2</reference>. The grace of God works upon the will and affections by renewing the understanding. Light is the first thing in the new creation, as it was in the first: <hi type="italic">after the image of him who created him.</hi> It was the honour of man in innocence that he was made after the image of God; but that image was defaced and lost by sin, and is renewed by sanctifying grace: so that a renewed soul is something like what Adam was in the day he was created. In the privilege and duty of sanctification <hi type="italic">there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">v. 11</reference>. There is now no difference arising from different country or different condition and circumstance of life: it is as much the duty of the one as of the other to be holy, and as much the privilege of the one as of the other to receive from God the grace to be so. Christ came to take down all partition-walls, that all might stand on the same level before God, both in duty and privilege. And for this reason, because <hi type="italic">Christ is all in all.</hi> Christ is a Christian's all, his only Lord and Saviour, and all his hope and happiness. And to those who are sanctified, one as well as another and whatever they are in other respects, he is <hi type="italic">all in all,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Alpha</hi> and <hi type="italic">Omega,</hi> the <hi type="italic">beginning and the end:</hi> he is all in all things to them.
entries.b9f61c7b32fc49c587373eee04e987f91957fb9a: <div eID="gen32106" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Love Recommended. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32107" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; <hi type="super">13</hi> Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also <hi type="italic">do</hi> ye. <hi type="super">14</hi> And above all these things <hi type="italic">put on</hi> charity, which is the bond of perfectness. <hi type="super">15</hi> And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful. <hi type="super">16</hi> Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord. <hi type="super">17</hi> And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, <hi type="italic">do</hi> all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him. <div eID="gen32107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32108" type="x-p"/> The apostle proceeds to exhort to mutual love and compassion: <hi type="italic">Put on therefore bowels of mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.12">v. 12</reference>. We must not only put off anger and wrath (as <reference osisRef="Col.3.8">v. 8</reference>), but we must put on compassion and kindness; not only cease to do evil, but learn to do well; not only not do hurt to any, but do what good we can to all. <div eID="gen32108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32109" type="x-p"/> I. The argument here used to enforce the exhortation is very affecting: <hi type="italic">Put on, as the elect of God, holy and beloved.</hi> Observe, 1. Those who are holy are the elect of God; and those who are the elect of God, and holy, are beloved—beloved of God, and ought to be so of all men. 2. Those who are the elect of God, holy and beloved, ought to conduct themselves in every thing as becomes them, and so as not to lose the credit of their holiness, nor the comfort of their being chosen and beloved. It becomes those who are holy towards God to be lowly and loving towards all men. Observe, What we must put on in particular. (1.) Compassion towards the miserable: <hi type="italic">Bowels of mercy,</hi> the tenderest mercies. Those who owe so much to mercy ought to be merciful to all who are proper objects of mercy. <hi type="italic">Be you merciful, as your Father is merciful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.6.36">Luke vi. 36</reference>. (2.) <hi type="italic">Kindness</hi> towards our friends, and those who love us. A courteous disposition becomes the elect of God; for the design of the gospel is not only to soften the minds of men, but to sweeten them, and to promote friendship among men as well as reconciliation with God. (3.) <hi type="italic">Humbleness of mind,</hi> in submission to those above us, and condescension to those below us. There must not only be a humble demeanour, but a humble mind. <hi type="italic">Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Matt. xi. 29</reference>. (4.) <hi type="italic">Meekness</hi> towards those who have provoked us, or been any way injurious to us. We must not be transported into any indecency by our resentment of indignities and neglects: but must prudently bridle our own anger, and patiently bear the anger of others. (5.) <hi type="italic">Long-suffering</hi> towards those who continue to provoke us. <hi type="italic">Charity suffereth long,</hi> as well <hi type="italic">as is kind,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.4">1 Cor. xiii. 4</reference>. Many can bear a short provocation who are weary of bearing when it grows long. But we must suffer long both the injuries of men and the rebukes of divine Providence. If God is long-suffering to us, under all our provocations of him, we should exercise long-suffering to others in like cases. (6.) Mutual forbearance, in consideration of the infirmities and deficiencies under which we all labour: <hi type="italic">Forbearing one another.</hi> We have all of us something which needs to be borne with, and this is a good reason why we should bear with others in what is disagreeable to us. We need the same good turn from others which we are bound to show them. (7.) A readiness to forgive injuries: <hi type="italic">Forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any.</hi> While we are in this world, where there is so much corruption in our hearts, and so much occasion of difference and contention, quarrels will sometimes happen, even among the elect of God, who are holy and beloved, as Paul and Barnabas had a <hi type="italic">sharp contention, which parted them asunder one from the other</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.39">Acts xv. 39</reference>), and Paul and Peter, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.14">Gal. ii. 14</reference>. But it is our duty to forgive one another in such cases; not to bear any grudge, but put up with the affront and pass it by. And the reason is: <hi type="italic">Even as Christ forgave you, so also do you.</hi> The consideration that we are forgiven by Christ so many offences is a good reason why we should forgive others. It is an argument of the divinity of Christ that he had <hi type="italic">power on earth to forgive sins;</hi> and it is a branch of his example which we are obliged to follow, if we ourselves would be forgiven. <hi type="italic">Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.12">Matt. vi. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen32109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32110" type="x-p"/> II. In order to all this, we are exhorted here to several things:—1. To clothe ourselves with love (<reference osisRef="Col.3.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Above all things put on charity:</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epi pasi de toutois</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">over all things.</hi> Let this be the upper garment, the robe, the livery, the mark of our dignity and distinction. Or, Let this be principal and chief, as the whole sum and abstract of the second table. <hi type="italic">Add to faith virtue, and to brotherly-kindness charity,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.5-2Pet.1.7">2 Pet. i. 5-7</reference>. He lays the foundation in faith, and the top-stone in charity, <hi type="italic">which is the bond of perfectness,</hi> the cement and centre of all happy society. Christian unity consists of unanimity and mutual love. 2. To submit ourselves to the government of the <hi type="italic">peace of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.3.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let the peace of God rule in your hearts,</hi> that is, God's being at peace with you, and the comfortable sense of his acceptance and favour: or, a disposition to peace among yourselves, a peaceable spirit, that keeps the peace, and makes peace. This is called the <hi type="italic">peace of God,</hi> because it is of his working in all who are his. The <hi type="italic">kingdom of God is righteousness and peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Rom. xiv. 17</reference>. "Let this peace <hi type="italic">rule in your heart</hi>—prevail and govern there, or as an umpire decide all matters of difference among you."—<hi type="italic">To which you are called in one body.</hi> We are called to this peace, to peace with God as our privilege and peace with our brethren as our duty. Being united in one body, we are called to be at peace one with another, as the members of the natural body; for <hi type="italic">we are the body of Christ, and members in particular,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.27">1 Cor. xii. 27</reference>. To preserve in us this peaceable disposition, we must be thankful. The work of thanksgiving to God is such a sweet and pleasant work that it will help to make us sweet and pleasant towards all men. "Instead of envying one another upon account of any particular favours and excellence, be thankful for his mercies, which are common to all of you." 3. To let the <hi type="italic">word of Christ dwell in us richly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.16">v. 16</reference>. The gospel is the word of Christ, which has come to us; but that is not enough, it must dwell in us, or <hi type="italic">keep house</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">enoikeito,</hi></hi> not as a servant in a family, who is under another's control, but as a master, who has a right to prescribe to and direct all under his roof. We must take our instructions and directions from it, and our portion of meat and strength, of grace and comfort, in due season, as from the <hi type="italic">master of the household.</hi> It must dwell in us; that is, be always ready and at hand to us in every thing, and have its due influence and use. We must be familiarly acquainted with it, and <hi type="italic">know it for our good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.5.27">Job v. 27</reference>. It must dwell in us richly: not only keep house in our hearts, but keep a good house. Many have the word of Christ dwelling in them, but it dwells in them but poorly; it has no mighty force and influence upon them. Then the soul prospers when the word of God <hi type="italic">dwells in us richly,</hi> when we have abundance of it in us, and are full of the scriptures and of the grace of Christ. And this in all wisdom. The proper office of wisdom is to apply what we know to ourselves, for our own direction. The word of Christ must dwell in us, not in all notion and speculation, to make us doctors, but in all wisdom, to make us good Christians, and enable us to conduct ourselves in every thing as becomes Wisdom's children. 4. To teach and admonish one another. This would contribute very much to our furtherance in all grace; for we sharpen ourselves by quickening others, and improve our knowledge by communicating it for their edification. We must <hi type="italic">admonish one another in psalms and hymns.</hi> Observe, Singing of psalms is a gospel ordinance: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">psalmois kai hymnois kai odais</hi></hi>—the Psalms of David, and spiritual hymns and odes, collected out of the scripture, and suited to special occasions, instead of their lewd and profane songs in their idolatrous worship. Religious poesy seems countenanced by these expressions and is capable of great edification. But, when we sing psalms, we make no melody unless we sing with grace in our hearts, unless we are suitably affected with what we sing and go along in it with true devotion and understanding. Singing of psalms is a teaching ordinance as well as a praising ordinance; and we are not only to quicken and encourage ourselves, but to <hi type="italic">teach and admonish one another,</hi> mutually excite our affections, and convey instructions. 5. All must be done in the name of Christ (<reference osisRef="Col.3.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">And whatsoever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus,</hi> according to his command and in compliance with his authority, by strength derived from him, with an eye to his glory, and depending upon his merit for the acceptance of what is good and the pardon of what is amiss, <hi type="italic">Giving thanks to God and the Father by him.</hi> Observe, (1.) We must give thanks in all things; whatsoever we do, we must still give thanks, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.20">Eph. v. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">Giving thanks always for all things.</hi> (2.) The Lord Jesus must be the Mediator of our praises as well as of our prayers. <hi type="italic">We give thanks to God and the Father in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.20">Eph. v. 20</reference>. Those who do all things in Christ's name will never want matter of thanksgiving to God, even the Father.
entries.ebd0b8403806e3156b81248feaf714e21f2f1e44: <div eID="gen32110" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Relative Duties. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32111" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord. <hi type="super">19</hi> Husbands, love <hi type="italic">your</hi> wives, and be not bitter against them. <hi type="super">20</hi> Children, obey <hi type="italic">your</hi> parents in all things: for this is well pleasing unto the Lord. <hi type="super">21</hi> Fathers, provoke not your children <hi type="italic">to anger,</hi> lest they be discouraged. <hi type="super">22</hi> Servants, obey in all things <hi type="italic">your</hi> masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God: <hi type="super">23</hi> And whatsoever ye do, do <hi type="italic">it</hi> heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; <hi type="super">24</hi> Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ. <hi type="super">25</hi> But he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons. <div eID="gen32111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32112" type="x-p"/> The apostle concludes the chapter with exhortations to relative duties, as before in the epistle to the Ephesians. The epistles which are most taken up in displaying the glory of divine grace, and magnifying the Lord Jesus, are the most particular and distinct in pressing the duties of the several relations. We must never separate the privileges and duties of the gospel religion. <div eID="gen32112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32113" type="x-p"/> I. He begins with the duties of wives and husbands (<reference osisRef="Col.3.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord.</hi> Submission is the duty of wives, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hypotassesthe.</hi></hi> It is the same word which is used to express our duty to magistrates (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Rom. xiii. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">Let every soul be</hi> subject <hi type="italic">to the higher powers</hi>), and is expressed by subjection and reverence, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.24">Eph. v. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.33">33</reference>. The reason is that <hi type="italic">Adam was first formed, then Eve: and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, being deceived, was in the transgression,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.13-1Tim.2.14">1 Tim. ii. 13, 14</reference>. He was first in the creation and last in the transgression. The <hi type="italic">head of the woman is the man;</hi> and the <hi type="italic">man is not of the woman, but the woman of the man; neither was the man created for the woman, but the woman for the man,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.3">1 Cor. xi. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.8">8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.9">9</reference>. It is agreeable to the order of nature and the reason of things, as well as the appointment and will of God. But then it is submission, not to a rigorous lord or absolute tyrant, who may do his will and is without restraints, but to a husband, and to her own husband, who stands in the nearest relation, and is under strict engagements to proper duty too. And <hi type="italic">this is fit in the Lord,</hi> it is becoming the relation, and what they are bound in duty to do, as an instance of obedience to the authority and law of Christ. On the other hand, <hi type="italic">husbands must love their wives, and not be bitter against them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.19">v. 19</reference>. They must love them with tender and faithful affection, as Christ loved the church, and as their own bodies, and even as themselves (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.25">Eph. v. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.28">28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.33">33</reference>), with a love peculiar to the nearest relation and the greatest comfort and blessing of life. And they must not be bitter against them, not use them unkindly, with harsh language or severe treatment, but be kind and obliging to them in all things; for the <hi type="italic">woman was made for the man, neither is the man without the woman,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">man also is by the woman,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.9">1 Cor. xi. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.11">11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.12">12</reference>. <div eID="gen32113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32114" type="x-p"/> II. The duties of children and parents: <hi type="italic">Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is well-pleasing unto the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.20">v. 20</reference>. They must be willing to do all their lawful commands, and be at their direction and disposal; as those who have a natural right and are fitter to direct them than themselves. The apostle (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.2">Eph. vi. 2</reference>) requires them to honour as well as obey their parents; they must esteem them and think honourably of them, as the obedience of their lives must proceed from the esteem and opinion of their minds. And this is <hi type="italic">well-pleasing to God,</hi> or acceptable to him; for it is the <hi type="italic">first commandment with promise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.2">Eph. vi. 2</reference>), with an explicit promise annexed to it, namely, <hi type="italic">That it shall be well with them, and they shall live long on the earth.</hi> Dutiful children are the most likely to prosper in the world and enjoy long life. And parents must be tender, as well as children obedient (<reference osisRef="Col.3.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged.</hi> Let not your authority over them be exercised with rigour and severity, but with kindness and gentleness, lest you raise their passions and discourage them in their duty, and by holding the reins too tight make them fly out with greater fierceness." The bad temper and example of imprudent parents often prove a great hindrance to their children and a stumbling-block in their way; see <reference osisRef="Eph.6.4">Eph. vi. 4</reference>. And it is by the tenderness of parents, and dutifulness of children, that God ordinarily furnishes his church with a seed to serve him, and propagates religion from age to age. <div eID="gen32114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32115" type="x-p"/> III. Servants and masters: <hi type="italic">Servants, obey your masters in all things according to the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.22">v. 22</reference>. Servants must do the duty of the relation in which they stand, and obey their master's commands in <hi type="italic">all things</hi> which are consistent with their duty to God their heavenly Master. <hi type="italic">Not with eye-service, as men-pleasers</hi>—not only when their master's eye is upon them, but when they are from under their master's eye. They must be both just and diligent. <hi type="italic">In singleness of heart, fearing God</hi>—without selfish designs, or hypocrisy and disguise, as those who fear God and stand in awe of him. Observe, The fear of God ruling in the heart will make people good in every relation. Servants who fear God will be just and faithful when they are from under their master's eye, because they know they are under the eye of God. See <reference osisRef="Gen.20.11">Gen. xx. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Because I thought, Surely the fear of God is not in this place.</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.5.15">Neh. v. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">But so did not I, because of the fear of God.</hi> "And <hi type="italic">whatsoever you do, do it heartily</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.3.23">v. 23</reference>), with diligence, not idly and slothfully:" or, "Do it cheerfully, not discontented at the providence of God which put you in that relation."—<hi type="italic">As to the Lord, and not as to men.</hi> It sanctifies a servant's work when it is done as unto God—with an eye to his glory and in obedience to his command, and not merely as unto men, or with regard to them only. Observe, We are really doing our duty to God when we are faithful in our duty to men. And, for servants' encouragement, let them know that a good and faithful servant is never the further from heaven for his being a servant: "<hi type="italic">Knowing that of the Lord you shall receive the reward of the inheritance, for you serve the Lord Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.24">v. 24</reference>. Serving your masters according to the command of Christ, you serve Christ, and he will be your paymaster: you will have a glorious reward at last. Though you are now servants, you will receive the inheritance of sons. But, on the other hand, <hi type="italic">He who does wrong will receive for the wrong which he has done,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Col.3.25">v. 25</reference>. There is a righteous God, who, if servants wrong their masters, will reckon with them for it, though they may conceal it from their master's notice. And he will be sure to punish the unjust as well as reward the faithful servant: and so if masters wrong their servants.—<hi type="italic">And there is no respect of persons with him.</hi> The righteous Judge of the earth will be impartial, and carry it with an equal hand towards the master and servant; not swayed by any regard to men's outward circumstances and condition of life. The one and the other will stand upon a level at his tribunal. <div eID="gen32115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32116" type="x-p"/> It is probable that the apostle has a particular respect, in all these instances of duty, to the case mentioned <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.1-1Cor.7.40">1 Cor. vii.</reference> of relations of a different religion, as a Christian and heathen, a Jewish convert and an uncircumcised Gentile, where there was room to doubt whether they were bound to fulfil the proper duties of their several relations to such persons. And, if it hold in such cases, it is much stronger upon Christians one towards another, and where both are of the same religion. And how happy would the gospel religion make the world, if it every where prevailed; and how much would it influence every state of things and every relation of life!  <chapter eID="Col.3"/> <div eID="gen32116" type="x-p"/>

entries.e6e434c1c11161561da26bf9e4c928d9e4815ca3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17877"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Col.3.1-Col.3.25">Col 3:1-25</reference>. Exhortations to Heavenly Aims, as Opposed to Earthly, on the Ground of Union to the Risen Saviour; to Mortify and Put Off the Old Man, and to Put on the New; in Charity, Humility, Words of Edification, Thankfulness; Relative Duties.</title> <div sID="gen36434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17877"/><hi type="bold">1. If ... then--</hi>The connection with <reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>, 23, is, he had condemned the "fleshly mind" and the "satiating to the full the flesh"; in contrast to this he now says, "If then ye have been once for all raised up (Greek, aorist tense) together with Christ" (namely, at your conversion and baptism, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.4">Ro 6:4</reference>).<div eID="gen36434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek those things ... above--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">Mt 6:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>).<div eID="gen36435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sitteth--</hi>rather, as Greek, "Where Christ is, sitting on the right of God" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.20">Ep 1:20</reference>). The Head being quickened, the members are also quickened with Him. Where the Head is, there the members must be. The contrast is between the believer's former state, alive to the world but dead to God, and his present state, dead to the world but alive to God; and between the earthly abode of the unbeliever and the heavenly abode of the believer (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.47">1Co 15:47</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.48">48</reference>). We are already seated there in Him as our Head; and hereafter shall be seated by Him, as the Bestower of our bliss. As Elisha (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.2">2Ki 2:2</reference>) said to Elijah when about to ascend, "As the Lord liveth ... I will not leave thee"; so we must follow the ascended Saviour with the wings of our meditations and the chariots of our affections. We should trample upon and subdue our lusts that our conversation may correspond to our Saviour's condition; that where the eyes of apostles were forced to leave Him, thither our thoughts may follow Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.21">Mt 6:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.32">Joh 12:32</reference>) [Pearson]. Of ourselves we can no more ascend than a bar of iron lift itself up' from the earth. But the love of Christ is a powerful magnet to draw us up (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.5">Ep 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.6">6</reference>). The design of the Gospel is not merely to give rules, but mainly to supply motives to holiness. <div eID="gen36436" type="x-p"/>
entries.93d6644eca2d763eb270d84a1a5480eb5180aa6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17878"/><div sID="gen36437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17878"/>2. Translate, "Set your mind on the things above, not on the things," &c. (<reference osisRef="Col.2.20">Col 2:20</reference>). Contrast "who mind earthly things" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>). Whatever we make an idol of, will either be a cross to us if we be believers, or a curse to us if unbelievers. <div eID="gen36437" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f145b1cd9dee46eb7b4a72638fb209ce3bb441f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17879"/><div sID="gen36438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17879"/>3. The Greek aorist tense implies, "For ye have died once for all" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.6.4-Rom.6.7">Ro 6:4-7</reference>). It is not said, Ye must die practically to the world in order to become dead with Christ; but the latter is assumed as once for all having taken place in the regeneration; what believers are told is, Develop this spiritual life in practice. "No one longs for eternal, incorruptible, and immortal life, unless he be wearied of this temporal, corruptible, and mortal life" [Augustine].<div eID="gen36438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and your life ... hid--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.83.3">Psa 83:3</reference>); like a seed buried in the earth; compare "planted," <reference osisRef="Rom.6.5">Ro 6:5</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.13.31">Mt 13:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.33">33</reference>, "like ... leaven ... hid." As the glory of Christ now is hid from the world, so also the glory of believers' inner life, proceeding from communion with Him, is still hidden with Christ in God; but (<reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col 3:4</reference>) when Christ, the Source of this life, shall manifest Himself in glory, then shall their hidden glory be manifest, and correspond in appearance to its original [Neander]. The Christian's secret communion with God will now at times make itself seen without his intending it (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.14">Mt 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">16</reference>); but his full manifestation is at Christ's manifestation (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">Mt 13:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.19-Rom.8.23">Ro 8:19-23</reference>). "It doth not yet appear (Greek, 'is not yet manifested') what we shall be" (<reference osisRef="1John.3.2">1Jo 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1Pe 1:7</reference>). As yet Christians do not always recognize the "life" of one another, so hidden is it, and even at times doubt as to their own life, so weak is it, and so harassed with temptations (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.1-Ps.51.19">Psa 51:1-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.1-Rom.7.25">Ro 7:1-25</reference>).<div eID="gen36439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in God--</hi>to whom Christ has ascended. Our "life" is "laid up for" us in God (<reference osisRef="Col.1.5">Col 1:5</reference>), and is secured by the decree of Him who is invisible to the world (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>). <div eID="gen36440" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc41af8c783b40174559f03d870164900c51de64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17880"/><div sID="gen36441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17880"/>4. Translate, "When Christ shall be manifested who is our life (<reference osisRef="John.11.25">Joh 11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.6">14:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.19">19</reference>), then shall ye also with Him be manifested in glory" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.13">1Pe 4:13</reference>). The spiritual life our souls have now in Him shall be extended to our bodies (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>).<div eID="gen36441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>and not till then. Those err who think to find a perfect Church before then. The true Church is now militant. Rome errs in trying to set up a Church now regnant and triumphant. The true Church shall be visible as a perfect and reigning Church, when Christ shall be visibly manifested as her reigning Head. Rome having ceased to look for Him in patient faith, has set up a visible mockhead, a false anticipation of the millennial kingdom. The Papacy took to itself by robbery that glory which is an object of hope, and can only be reached by bearing the cross now. When the Church became a harlot, she ceased to be a bride who goes to meet her Bridegroom. Hence the millennial kingdom ceased to be looked for [Auberlen]. <div eID="gen36442" type="x-p"/>
entries.af0317d931a7278715a5ef3667fc1990e2e58cc8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17881"/><div sID="gen36443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17881"/><hi type="bold">5. Mortify--</hi>Greek, "make a corpse of"; "make dead"; "put to death."<div eID="gen36443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col 3:3</reference>). Follow out to its necessary consequence the fact of your having once for all died with Christ spiritually at your regeneration, by daily "deadening your members," of which united "the body of the sins of the flesh" consists (compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.11">Col 2:11</reference>). "The members" to be mortified are the fleshly instruments of lust, in so far as the members of the body are abused to such purposes. Habitually repress and do violence to corrupt desires of which the members are the instruments (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.6.19">Ro 6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.13">8:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.24">Ga 5:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen36444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the earth--</hi>where they find their support [Bengel] (Compare <reference osisRef="Col.3.2">Col 3:2</reference>, "things on earth"). See <reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Ep 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.4">4</reference>.<div eID="gen36445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inordinate affection--</hi>"lustful passion."<div eID="gen36446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil concupiscence--</hi>more general than the last [Alford], the disorder of the external senses; "lustful passion," lust within [Bengel].<div eID="gen36447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covetousness--</hi>marked off by the Greek article as forming a whole genus by itself, distinct from the genus containing the various species just enumerated. It implies a self-idolizing, grasping spirit; far worse than another Greek term translated "the love of money" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">1Ti 6:10</reference>).<div eID="gen36448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36449" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is--</hi>that is, inasmuch as it is "idolatry." Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Eph.4.19">Ep 4:19</reference>, on its connection with sins of impurity. Self and mammon are deified in the heart instead of God (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.24">Mt 6:24</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">Ep 5:5</reference>). <div eID="gen36449" type="x-p"/>
entries.773747b4e202f9cf57996c9d3659762b91a4a959: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17882"/><div sID="gen36450" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17882"/>6. (See on <reference osisRef="Eph.5.6">Ep 5:6</reference>.) <div eID="gen36450" type="x-p"/>
entries.854d8e2b1ab902613ab51b67a17371787d7f43e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17883"/><div sID="gen36451" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17883"/><hi type="bold">7. sometime--</hi>"once."<div eID="gen36451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walked ... when ye lived in them--</hi>These sins were the very element in which ye "lived" (before ye became once for all dead with Christ to them); no wonder, then, that ye "walked" in them. Compare on the opposite side, "living in the Spirit," having as its legitimate consequence, "walking in the Spirit" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.25">Ga 5:25</reference>). The "living" comes first in both cases, the walking follows. <div eID="gen36452" type="x-p"/>
entries.f368363bb94f62c9980fa362f2b9f44d7d74134f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17884"/><div sID="gen36453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17884"/><hi type="bold">8. But now--</hi>that ye are no longer living in them.<div eID="gen36453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye also--</hi>like other believers; answering to "ye also" (<reference osisRef="Col.3.7">Col 3:7</reference>) like other unbelievers formerly.<div eID="gen36454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put off--</hi>"Do ye also put away all these," namely, those just enumerated, and those which follow [Alford].<div eID="gen36455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anger, wrath--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Eph.4.31">Ep 4:31</reference>).<div eID="gen36456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blasphemy--</hi>rather, "reviling," "evil-speaking," as it is translated in <reference osisRef="Eph.4.31">Ep 4:31</reference>.<div eID="gen36457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filthy communication--</hi>The context favors the translation, "abusive language," rather than impure conversation. "Foul language" best retains the ambiguity of the original. <div eID="gen36458" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a532bb9729d60f5e32fcaddecf931abc66f78b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17885"/><div sID="gen36459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17885"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.25">Ep 4:25</reference>.)<div eID="gen36459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put off--</hi>Greek, "wholly put off"; utterly renounced [Tittmann]. (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.22">Ep 4:22</reference>).<div eID="gen36460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the old man--</hi>the unregenerate nature which ye had before conversion.<div eID="gen36461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his deeds--</hi>habits of acting. <div eID="gen36462" type="x-p"/>
entries.1bc703127e410b6344938ee443d90b9d40ba267e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17886"/><div sID="gen36463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17886"/><hi type="bold">10. the new man--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Eph.4.23">Ep 4:23</reference>). Here (neon) the Greek, means "the recently-put-on nature"; that lately received at regeneration (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.4.23">Ep 4:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen36463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is renewed--</hi>Greek, "which is being renewed" (anakainottmenou); namely, its development into a perfectly renewed nature is continually progressing to completion.<div eID="gen36464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in knowledge--</hi>rather as the Greek, "unto perfect knowledge" (see on <reference osisRef="Col.1.6">Col 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.9">Col 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>). Perfect knowledge of God excludes all sin (<reference osisRef="John.17.3">Joh 17:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after the image of him that created him--</hi>namely, of God that created the new man (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>; 4:24). The new creation is analogous to the first creation (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2Co 4:6</reference>). As man was then made in the image of God naturally, so now spiritually. But the image of God formed in us by the Spirit of God, is as much more glorious than that borne by Adam, as the Second Man, the Lord from heaven, is more glorious than the first man. <reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Ge 1:26</reference>, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." The "image" is claimed for man, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.7">1Co 11:7</reference>; the "likeness," <reference osisRef="Jas.3.9">Jas 3:9</reference>. Origen [On First Principles, 3:6] taught, the image was something in which all were created, and which continued to man after the fall (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Ge 9:6</reference>). The likeness was something towards which man was created, that he might strive after it and attain it. Trench thinks God in the double statement (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Ge 1:26</reference>), contemplates both man's first creation and his being "renewed in knowledge after the image of Him that created Him." <div eID="gen36466" type="x-p"/>
entries.adfb8205f913c0c0edf7ce284efec31f42d23412: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17887"/><div sID="gen36467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17887"/><hi type="bold">11. Where--</hi>Translate, "Wherein," namely, in the sphere of the renewed man.<div eID="gen36467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... nor ... nor ... nor--</hi>Translate as Greek, "There is no such thing as Greek and Jew (the difference of privilege between those born of the natural seed of Abraham and those not, is abolished), circumcision and uncircumcision (the difference of legal standing between the circumcised and uncircumcised is done away, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.15">Ga 6:15</reference>)--bondman, freeman." The present Church is one called out of the flesh, and the present world-course (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>), wherein such distinctions exist, to life in the Spirit, and to the future first resurrection: and this because Satan has such power now over the flesh and the world. At Christ's coming when Satan shall no longer rule the flesh and the world, the nations in the flesh, and the word in millennial felicity, shall be the willing subjects of Christ and His glorified saints (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Da 7:14</reference>, 22, 27; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.17">Lu 19:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.1-Rev.6.3">Re 20:1-6; 3</reference>:21). Israel in Canaan was a type of that future state when the Jews, so miraculously preserved distinct now in their dispersion, shall be the central Church of the Christianized world. As expressly as Scripture abolishes the distinction of Jew and Greek now as to religious privileges, so does it expressly foretell that in the coming new order of things, Israel shall be first of the Christian nations, not for her own selfish aggrandizement, but for their good, as the medium of blessing to them. Finally, after the millennium, the life that is in Christ becomes the power which transfigures nature, in the time of the new heaven and the new earth; as, before, it first transfigured the spiritual, then the political and social world.<div eID="gen36468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Scythian--</hi>heretofore regarded as more barbarian than the barbarians. Though the relation of bond and free actually existed, yet in relation to Christ, all alike were free in one aspect, and servants of Christ in another (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">1Co 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Ga 3:28</reference>).<div eID="gen36469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36470" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ is all--</hi>Christ absorbs in Himself all distinctions, being to all alike, everything that they need for justification, sanctification, and glorification (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21-1Cor.3.23">3:21-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>).<div eID="gen36470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all--</hi>who believe and are renewed, without distinction of person; the sole distinction now is, how much each draws from Christ. The unity of the divine life shared in by all believers, counterbalances all differences, even as great as that between the polished "Greek" and the rude "Scythian." Christianity imparts to the most uncivilized the only spring of sound, social and moral culture. <div eID="gen36471" type="x-p"/>
entries.429c389ce32e58e2d7b70aebd00aaed465e91b66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17888"/><div sID="gen36472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17888"/><hi type="bold">12. the elect of God--</hi>There is no "the" in the Greek, "God's elect" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Ro 8:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.4">1Th 1:4</reference>). The order of the words "elect, holy, beloved," answers to the order of the things. Election from eternity precedes sanctification in time; the sanctified, feeling God's love, imitate it [Bengel].<div eID="gen36472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bowels of mercies--</hi>Some of the oldest manuscripts read singular, "mercy." Bowels express the yearning compassion, which has its seat in the heart, and which we feel to act on our inward parts (<reference osisRef="Gen.43.30">Ge 43:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jr 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.78">Lu 1:78</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen36473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">humbleness of mind--</hi>True "lowliness of mind"; not the mock "humility" of the false teachers (<reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.2">Ep 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.32">32</reference>). <div eID="gen36474" type="x-p"/>
entries.f25c5afa89f3b5c396530e75343dedfd21aa5743: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17889"/><div sID="gen36475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17889"/><hi type="bold">13. Forbearing--</hi>as to present offenses.<div eID="gen36475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgiving--</hi>as to past offenses.<div eID="gen36476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quarrel--</hi>rather as Greek, "cause of blame," "cause of complaint."<div eID="gen36477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ--</hi>who had so infinitely greater cause of complaint against us. The oldest manuscripts and Vulgate read "the Lord." English Version is supported by one very old manuscript and old versions. It seems to have crept in from <reference osisRef="Eph.4.32">Ep 4:32</reference>. <div eID="gen36478" type="x-p"/>
entries.ecc3648011331a1655450cb43c1e83ee98a4b96c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17890"/><div sID="gen36479" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17890"/><hi type="bold">14. above--</hi>rather "over," as in <reference osisRef="Eph.6.16">Ep 6:16</reference>. Charity, which is the crowning grace, covering the multitude of others' sins (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">1Pe 4:8</reference>), must overlie all the other graces enumerated.<div eID="gen36479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is--</hi>that is, "for it is"; literally, "which thing is."<div eID="gen36480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bond of perfectness--</hi>an upper garment which completes and keeps together the rest, which, without it, would be loose and disconnected. Seeming graces, where love is wanting, are mere hypocrisy. Justification by faith is assumed as already having taken place in those whom Paul addresses, <reference osisRef="Col.3.12">Col 3:12</reference>, "elect of God, holy ... beloved," and <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>; so that there is no plea here for Rome's view of justification by works. Love and its works "perfect," that is, manifest the full maturity of faith developed (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Mt 5:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.48">48</reference>). Love ... be ye perfect, &c. (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.21">Jas 2:21</reference>, 22; <reference osisRef="1John.2.5">1Jo 2:5</reference>). "If we love one another, God's love is perfected in us" (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.8">Ro 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.13">1Co 13:1-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.12">1Jo 4:12</reference>). As to "bond," compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>, "knit together in love" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.3">Ep 4:3</reference>), "keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." <div eID="gen36481" type="x-p"/>
entries.ccba5b8e9652006af5c381cfaf414a2fc892aaae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17891"/><div sID="gen36482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17891"/><hi type="bold">15. peace of God--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and versions read, "The peace of Christ" (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Php 4:7</reference>). "The peace of God." Therefore Christ is God. Peace was His legacy to His disciples before He left them (<reference osisRef="John.14.27">Joh 14:27</reference>), "My peace I give unto you." Peace is peculiarly His to give. Peace follows love (<reference osisRef="Col.3.14">Col 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.2">Ep 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen36482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rule--</hi>literally, "sit as umpire"; the same Greek verb simple, as appears compounded (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>). The false teacher, as a self-constituted umpire, defrauds you of your prize; but if the peace of Christ be your umpire ruling in your hearts, your reward is sure. "Let the peace of Christ act as umpire when anger, envy, and such passions arise; and restrain them." Let not those passions give the award, so that you should be swayed by them, but let Christ's peace be the decider of everything.<div eID="gen36483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in your hearts--</hi>Many wear a peaceful countenance and speak peace with the mouth, while war is in their hearts (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.3">Psa 28:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.21">55:21</reference>).<div eID="gen36484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36485" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the which--</hi>that is, with a view to which state of Christian peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Is 26:3</reference>); <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.15">1Co 7:15</reference>, "God hath called us to peace."<div eID="gen36485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye are called--</hi>Greek, "ye were also called." The "also" implies that besides Paul's exhortation, they have also as a motive to "peace," their having been once for all called.<div eID="gen36486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in one body--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.4.4">Ep 4:4</reference>). The unity of the body is a strong argument for "peace" among the members.<div eID="gen36487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be ye thankful--</hi>for your "calling." Not to have "peace ruling in your hearts" would be inconsistent with the "calling in one body," and would be practical unthankfulness to God who called us (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.4">Ep 5:4</reference>, 19, 20). <div eID="gen36488" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8927cf3d14c8f5ba34e2ac6e38e128920fc57f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17892"/><div sID="gen36489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17892"/>16. The form which "thankfulness" (<reference osisRef="Col.3.15">Col 3:15</reference>) ought to take.<div eID="gen36489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Let the word of Christ--</hi>the Gospel word by which ye have been called.<div eID="gen36490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">richly--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.14">Ro 15:14</reference>).<div eID="gen36491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all wisdom--</hi>Alford joins this clause with "teaching," &c., not with "dwell in you," as English Version, for so we find in <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col 1:28</reference>, "teaching in all wisdom," and the two clauses will thus correspond, "In all wisdom teaching," and "in grace singing in your hears" (so the Greek order).<div eID="gen36492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ... and--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read "psalms, hymns, spiritual songs" (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">Ep 5:19</reference>). At the Agapæ or love-feasts, and in their family circles, they were to be so full of the Word of Christ in the heart that the mouth should give it utterance in hymns of instruction, admonition, and praise (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">De 6:7</reference>). Tertullian [Apology, 39], records that at the love-feasts, after the water had been furnished for the hands and the lights had been literally, according as any had the power, whether by his remembrance of Scripture, or by his powers of composition, he used to be invited to sing praises to God for the common good. Paul contrasts (as in <reference osisRef="Eph.5.18">Ep 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">19</reference>) the songs of Christians at their social meetings, with the bacchanalian and licentious songs of heathen feasts. Singing usually formed part of the entertainment at Greek banquets (compare <reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">Jas 5:13</reference>).<div eID="gen36493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with grace--</hi>Greek, "IN grace," the element in which your singing is to be: "the grace" of the indwelling Holy Spirit. This clause expresses the seat and source of true psalmody, whether in private or public, namely, the heart as well as the voice; singing (compare <reference osisRef="Col.3.15">Col 3:15</reference>, "peace ... rule in your hearts"), the psalm of love and praise being in the heart before it finds vent by the lips, and even when it is not actually expressed by the voice, as in closet-worship. The Greek order forbids English Version, "with grace in your hearts"; rather, "singing in your hearts."<div eID="gen36494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the Lord--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "to God." <div eID="gen36495" type="x-p"/>
entries.39c483fbd5c07267c39b396343d575905eb16f3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17893"/><div sID="gen36496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17893"/>17. Literally, "And everything whatsoever ye do ... do all," &c.; this includes words as well as deeds.<div eID="gen36496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the name of the Lord Jesus--</hi>as disciples called by His name as His, seeking His guidance and help, and desiring to act so as to gain His approval (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.8">Ro 14:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1Co 10:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.15">2Co 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1Pe 4:11</reference>). Compare "in the Lord," <reference osisRef="Col.3.18">Col 3:18</reference>, and "Christ is all," <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col 3:11</reference>.<div eID="gen36497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God and the Father--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "and," which seems to have crept in from <reference osisRef="Eph.5.20">Ep 5:20</reference>.<div eID="gen36498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by him--</hi>Greek, "through Him" as the channel of His grace to us, and of our thanksgiving to Him (<reference osisRef="John.14.6">Joh 14:6</reference>, end). <div eID="gen36499" type="x-p"/>
entries.deca4fd703bcc27623e0a8703269bef89afc0496: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17894"/><div sID="gen36500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17894"/><hi type="bold">18. unto your own husbands--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "own," which crept in from <reference osisRef="Eph.5.22">Ep 5:22</reference>.<div eID="gen36500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as it is fit in the Lord--</hi>Greek, "was fit," implying that there was at Colosse some degree of failure in fulfilling this duty, "as it was your duty to have done as disciples of the Lord." <div eID="gen36501" type="x-p"/>
entries.3654a01ee4c7f64d6e67686c401b673070a35735: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17895"/><div sID="gen36502" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17895"/>19. (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.22-Eph.5.33">Ep 5:22-33</reference>.)<div eID="gen36502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be not bitter--</hi>ill-tempered and provoking. Many who are polite abroad, are rude and bitter at home because they are not afraid to be so there. <div eID="gen36503" type="x-p"/>
entries.98abe5781369d6592140b3d55ff1bde10263aa26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17896"/><div sID="gen36504" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17896"/>20. (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.1">Ep 6:1</reference>.)<div eID="gen36504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the Lord--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "IN the Lord," that is, this is acceptable to God when it is done in the Lord, namely, from the principle of faith, and as disciples in union with the Lord. <div eID="gen36505" type="x-p"/>
entries.36dc4bb16412cf5e70bc9e950c9bfb14401417c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17897"/><div sID="gen36506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17897"/>21. (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.4">Ep 6:4</reference>.) It is a different Greek verb, therefore translate here, "irritate not." By perpetual fault-finding "children" are "discouraged" or "disheartened." A broken-down spirit is fatal to youth [Bengel]. <div eID="gen36506" type="x-p"/>
entries.732e9612a3137648d21769fe8f6297e61af665f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17898"/><div sID="gen36507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17898"/>22. (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">Ep 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.6">6</reference>.) This is to fear God, when, though none sees us, we do no evil: but if we do evil, it is not God, but men, whom we fear.<div eID="gen36507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">singleness--</hi>"simplicity of heart."<div eID="gen36508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fearing God--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "the Lord." <div eID="gen36509" type="x-p"/>
entries.740ad75e8c178eb4b94a1887cbb77ec3e03e192a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17899"/><div sID="gen36510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17899"/><hi type="bold">23. And--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.6.7">Ep 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.8">8</reference>). Compare the same principle in the case of all men, Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.31.21">2Ch 31:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.11">Ro 12:11</reference>).<div eID="gen36510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do, do it--</hi>two distinct Greek verbs, "Whatsoever ye do, work at it" (or "labor at" it).<div eID="gen36511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heartily--</hi>not from servile constraint, but with hearty good will. <div eID="gen36512" type="x-p"/>
entries.517ae327bf2e8abcb9a31abe481aa8b7a73854c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17900"/><div sID="gen36513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17900"/><hi type="bold">24. the reward of the inheritance--</hi>"Knowing that it is from the Lord (the ultimate source of reward), ye shall receive the compensation (or recompense, which will make ample amends for your having no earthly possession as slaves now) consisting of the inheritance" (a term excluding the notion of meriting it by works: it is all of grace, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.14">Ro 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.18">Ga 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen36513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ye serve--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "for," then translate as Vulgate, "Serve ye the Lord Christ;" compare <reference osisRef="Col.3.23">Col 3:23</reference>, "To the Lord and not unto men" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">1Co 7:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.23">23</reference>). <div eID="gen36514" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ada667a66b9a43456700fab667800e21700c4ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17901"/><div sID="gen36515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17901"/><hi type="bold">25. But--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "for," which accords with "serve ye," &c. (<reference osisRef="Col.3.24">Col 3:24</reference>), the oldest reading: the for here gives a motive for obeying the precept. He addresses the slaves: Serve ye the Lord Christ, and leave your wrongs in His hands to put to rights: (translate), "For he that doeth wrong shall receive back the wrong which he hath done (by just retribution in kind), and there is no respect of persons" with the Great Judge in the day of the Lord. He favors the master no more than the slave (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Re 6:15</reference>). <chapter eID="Col.3"/>

entries.7dce9f915ca225945ddef1a11d52afd62275570c: <div eID="gen50923" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen50924" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50925" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50925" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50924" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50926" type="x-p"/> The apostle exhorts the Colossians to heavenly-mindedness after the example of Christ, that they may be prepared to appear with him in glory, <reference osisRef="Col.3.1-Col.3.4">Col 3:1-4</reference>. Exhorts them also to mortify their members, and calls to their remembrance their former state, <reference osisRef="Col.3.5-Col.3.7">Col 3:5-7</reference>. Shows how completely they were changed from that state, and gives them various directions relative to truth, compassion, meekness, long-suffering, forgiveness, charity, <reference osisRef="Col.3.8-Col.3.14">Col 3:8-14</reference>. Shows that they are called to unity and holiness; and commands them to have the doctrine of Christ dwelling richly in them; and how they should teach and admonish each other, and do every thing, in the name of the Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="Col.3.15-Col.3.17">Col 3:15-17</reference>. The relative duties of wives, <reference osisRef="Col.3.18">Col 3:18</reference>. Of husbands, <reference osisRef="Col.3.19">Col 3:19</reference>.
